paragraphs: When photography arrived in the nineteenth century, many observers assumed that painters would lose their purpose, since a camera could record a scene faster and more accurately than any hand. The reverse happened. Freed from the obligation to document, painters turned toward what a camera could not do: they exaggerated color, flattened space and left their brushstrokes visible, treating the act of painting itself as a subject. Portraiture, long the steadiest source of income, shifted toward the expressive and the strange, and landscapes became records of a painter's perception rather than of a place. Photography did not end representational painting so much as force painters to ask what only painting could offer.
